facts.claim: Two critical PHP flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 ("PHP2Shell"), allow unauthenticated remote code execution; fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35.
Wiz timeline: first PHP bug found Aug 19, 2026; reported to PHP Aug 24; PHP acknowledged Sep 21; patched and disclosed Oct 21. Wiz used Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol.
Calif found multiple RCE paths Aug 1, 2026, reported first bug to PHP Aug 11. Calif credits OpenAI Patch the Planet for the invitation.
facts.note: Calif page itself says "No special harness, or access to models that weren't generally available"; Fortune/Wikipedia say GPT-5.6 Sol. Say "AI-assisted" and attribute the model to Fortune.

facts.claim: TIME: Wiz researcher Sagi Tzadik asked an AI agent to adapt a WordPress flaw to Drupal; after ~8 hours it reported failure, then said it had found a flaw in PHP. The weakness had gone undetected for more than a decade.
PHP is used by about 70% of websites (as reported by TIME, TechCrunch, Wiz; W3Techs ~69.2% of sites with a known server-side language per Wikipedia).

Amazon saw a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt in its MadPot honeypot on Oct 17, four days before disclosure; amazon says it is unclear how the actor got exploit information. The post does not attribute the activity to AI.
Leaks before the Oct 21 patch date pushed maintainers to release a day early; Calif mistakenly posted an exploit demo video.

Cloudflare: "tens of thousands" of exploit attempts within 45 minutes of the word getting out (reports broke late on Oct 20, ahead of the patch's official release), "hundreds of thousands" within two hours, and millions by the evening of Oct 21 (as reported by Fortune); Palo Alto Networks counted 22.6 million potentially vulnerable instances (Fortune).

Government sites in several countries (Czech Republic, Finland, Germany, Netherlands, per Reuters syndication) were taken offline as a precaution; NSA advised offline if unable to patch. Australia ACSC said it was not aware of active exploitation that day.
CISA said hackers are actively exploiting the two PHP bugs and ordered civilian federal agencies to patch within three days; it did not say who is exploiting them.

Dream (via The Hacker News): suspected China-nexus actor, low-to-moderate confidence, rooted 25 servers in US, Japan, Taiwan, South Korea, chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel flaw (CVE-2026-46300); Claude Code was found installed in the attack infrastructure and DeepSeek/Kimi API keys were configured.
facts.note: Evidence of AI tooling, not proof of how it was used; single-vendor report.

facts.claim: Palo Alto Unit 42 saw agentic-AI-style post-exploitation after PHP2Shell abuse, then retracted its link between a European government agency intrusion and PHP2Shell ("We are unable to confirm that initial access is associated with the specific PHP2Shell CVEs").
CrowdStrike (Oct 29): VAPOR PANDA ran ARTEX AI agents against 200+ organisations in 14+ countries over 11 days from Oct 17; confirmed post-exploitation at 9. NO source tied it to PHP2Shell.
facts.note: Primary CrowdStrike page not retrieved (403). Do not put on a slide until verified.

facts.claim: The "46" is a tracker count of states with ANY tracked item (moratorium, ban, zoning limit, executive order, pending/stalled/failed bill, tax-incentive pause): Electric Choice says "575 active restrictions across 46 states" (updated Oct 15, 2026). Four states have none: Alaska, Hawaii, West Virginia, Wyoming. It is NOT 46 states with statewide moratoriums.
facts.source: Electric Choice (Eisenbach Consulting) data-center moratorium tracker
facts.caveat: Tracker is internally inconsistent (46 state counts sum to 679, not 575; NC/GA counts differ between table and summary).

facts.claim: SAVRN (Sep 28, 2026): "46 states with state-level action" (192 state-level measures) - 29 restriction in force, 1 administrative pause, 11 pending, 5 failed/vetoed; 958 local jurisdictions; 49 states with local action. Includes non-moratoriums (e.g. Maryland and Nevada executive orders).
facts.source: SAVRN data center moratorium tracker update
facts.caveat: Read via a summarising fetch tool; per-state list not on the page.

facts.claim: New York Executive Order 62 (signed Jul 14, 2026) holds DEC environmental permits for data centers of 50 MW or more in abeyance for up to a year; exempts local approvals and manufacturing/research/education/medical uses. First statewide pause; a permit pause, not a ban on all construction.
facts.source: Beveridge & Diamond; SiliconANGLE; Davis Wright Tremaine

facts.claim: Texas: Gov. Abbott (Aug 3, 2026) halted approval of new data-center grid connections in ERCOT pending an audit; on Sep 21 he directed TCEQ to issue no data-center permits until the audit is done. Critics (incl. Ag Commissioner Sid Miller) say it falls short of a true moratorium; on-site-power projects and non-ERCOT areas not covered. As of Nov 4 the pause remains in place; audit expected to end in December.
facts.source: Route Fifty / Texas Tribune; gov.texas.gov; Texas Tribune Nov 4

facts.claim: Oregon: Gov. Kotek paused state-land requests for data centers (Sep 8, 2026, through Jul 1, 2027), then (Oct 13) directed DEQ to stop issuing air and water pollution permits for new or expanding data centers until July 2027, which OPB says would "effectively pause most data center development in Oregon". Her office says she cannot order a moratorium on private development without the Legislature.
Maine: legislature passed the first statewide data-center moratorium (Apr 14, 2026); Gov. Mills vetoed it Apr 24 and the override failed. So no state legislature has enacted a statewide moratorium.
facts.source: Reuters factbox via The Star; Electric Choice tracker
facts.caveat: Override failure from tracker; Tom's Hardware reported the bill as passed without noting the veto.

facts.claim: Virginia EO 22 (Sep 18, 2026) bans state NDAs on data centers and creates an AI task force; ending by-right approval for 25 MW+ is a PROPOSAL for the 2027 session. The Electric Choice tracker overstates it as an order that "ends by-right approval".

New Jersey local bans: counts vary by source - 6sqft says Jersey City is the 34th NJ municipality to ban data centers (Aug 2026); the Electric Choice tracker cites 93; Pinelands Alliance says 109 introduced or passed. Do not quote a precise NJ number.

S&P Global (Oct 1, 2026), via search summary: New York is the only state with a statewide moratorium (note: Texas and Oregon pauses are described as directives/audits); local governments in 40 states have an active ban or moratorium; voters face 34 data-center ballot measures in November (Ballotpedia).
facts.caveat: Page returns 403; numbers only via search summary. Do not put on a slide unless re-verified.

facts.claim: Local scale: GatherGov (Sep 2026) counts 632 jurisdictions with formal moratorium-related action since Jan 2026, 270 adopted a moratorium; durations mostly 6-12 months.
facts.caveat: From search summary only; definitions differ from other trackers.

facts.claim: LeCun's NIPS 2016 invited talk was titled 'Predictive Learning' (Posner Lecture); abstract: 'allowing machine to learn predictive models of the world is key to significant progress in artificial intelligence, and a necessary component of model-based planning and reinforcement learning'.

Synced: 'If intelligence is a cake, the bulk of the cake is unsupervised learning, the icing on the cake is supervised learning, and the cherry on the cake is reinforcement learning (RL).' LeCun's ISSCC 2019 update replaced 'unsupervised' with 'self-supervised'.

Nathan Lambert's RLHF Book lecture 5 maps the cake to LLMs: self-supervised learning on internet data = the bulk of the cake; supervised fine-tuning = the icing; reinforcement learning (RLHF, then RLVR) = the cherry; 'With agents, RL may be more than just the cherry in compute'. (Page shows no date.)

xAI on Grok 4: 'For Grok 4, we utilized Colossus, our 200,000 GPU cluster, to run reinforcement learning training that refines Grok's reasoning abilities at pretraining scale.' Also 'xAI will continue scaling reinforcement learning to unprecedented levels'. (Company claim.)

Epoch AI: 'OpenAI has said that o3 is a 10x scale-up in training compute from o1, almost certainly referring to reasoning training compute.' and Llama-Nemotron Ultra's RL stage 'took 140,000 H100-hours, or around 1e23 FLOP, <1% of the pre-training cost of the original base model.'
facts.source: Epoch AI Gradient Updates (Josh You), 'How far can reasoning models scale?'

facts.claim: Khatri et al.: 'DeepSeek-R1-Zero used 100,000 H800 GPU hours for RL training - 3.75% of its pre-training compute ... more than 10x increase from o1 to o3 ... and a similar leap from Grok-3 to Grok-4.'
facts.source: arXiv 2510.13786, 'The Art of Scaling Reinforcement Learning Compute for LLMs'

facts.claim: Karpathy: 'Running RLVR turned out to offer high capability/$, which gobbled up the compute that was originally intended for pretraining ... we saw ~similar sized LLMs but a lot longer RL runs.'
facts.source: Andrej Karpathy, '2025 LLM Year in Review'

facts.claim: DeepSeek-V3 technical report: pre-training costs 2664K H800 GPU hours, context extension 119K, post-training 5K; total 2.788M GPU hours (post-training about 0.2% of the total: our division).
Google DeepMind: 'Gemini Diffusion, is a state-of-the-art text diffusion model that learns to generate outputs by converting random noise into coherent text or code' (experimental research model).

Inception Labs: 'We are announcing the Mercury family of diffusion large language models (dLLMs)... Mercury is up to 10x faster than frontier speed-optimized LLMs' (vendor claim); 'coarse-to-fine' generation 'refined from pure noise over a few denoising steps'.

analogies.analogy: Pretraining is the lecture (the model reads everything and keeps guessing the next word). SFT is the worked examples in class (it copies good answers people wrote). RL is homework (it tries, gets graded by a reward model or by a checker, and tries again). Exams are the evaluations: they grade the model but do not teach it.
analogies.caveat: RL teaches with graded practice, but a benchmark exam does not change the model's dials unless someone trains on it. Label it as an analogy.

analogies.analogy: A CPU is a few professors who can solve any problem, one hard step at a time. A GPU is a stadium of thousands of students who each do a simple sum, all at the same moment. Training a network is millions of simple multiply-and-add sums, so the stadium wins.
analogies.mechanics_source: NVIDIA Hopper blog (16,896 CUDA cores), AMD product page (16 cores), bit-tech (MythBusters, 1,100 barrels)
analogies.caveat: A GPU core is simpler and slower than a CPU core; the claim is 'many simple workers', not '1,000 times faster'.

analogies.analogy: Supervised = flash cards with the answer on the back. Unsupervised = sorting a pile of one-sided cards into piles (or, with picture cards, drawing new cards that look like the pile). Reinforcement = training a dog with treats.
analogies.mechanics_source: CIFAR-10 page, k-means (Commons, Chire), OpenAI hide-and-seek (arXiv 1909.07528)
analogies.caveat: Generating new cards is generative modeling, usually trained with a denoising or next-piece target (self-supervised), a cousin of sorting rather than the same thing.

analogies.analogy: Cake = pretraining (self-supervised), icing = SFT, cherry = RL.
analogies.mechanics_source: LeCun slides 2016 and 2019 (via Synced); Nathan Lambert, RLHF Book lecture 5
analogies.status: community adaptation, not in LeCun's slides
analogies.caveat: LeCun's slides are about bits of feedback per example, not training stages; and by 2026 RL is no longer a small cherry by compute (estimates).
